findings.source_claim: Source describes usual Rajasthani ai→ē and au→ō, illustrating hē/hai, chēn compared with chain, and ōr compared with aur.
Source says i and u often change to a; preserve printed compared forms where supplied.
Source classifies these as dropping an aspirate; preserve the printed comparison pairs as attributed notes, not donor edges.
Root already flagged: taken called a Gujarati form; done also Gujarati. Both literal alternatives remain local attestations.
Source calls these the common Rajasthani contraction of verbs whose roots end in h; retain the explicit comparison forms rahē-hai, kahᵃṇō, rahyō.
Words elsewhere beginning b sometimes follow Gujarati in having w; wāt as well as bāt exemplifies the claim.
Source says Malvi has a decided but not universal dental preference over cerebral letters compared with Rangri; printed opposing forms remain attributed comparisons.

Source says ḍ is preferred to ṛ in specimens, sound fluctuates, and d/ḍ spelling is rather a matter of spelling; do not turn this into a mandatory phonemic merger. Source reports no observed neuter gender. Opening Ahiri/Ahir-wati naming discussion points to p49.
Oblique-base agent ending is compared explicitly with Gujarati, and the agent may occur before past intransitive/neuter verbs.
Source says the two genitives decline as in other Rajasthani dialects; kē/rē generally agree with a locative noun or, in Rangri, an agent noun; pitā-rē gharē is the example.

Excluded Malvi plural suffix comparison explicitly cites Khas of Nepal haru/heru and old Kanauji huār in Carey’s early-nineteenth-century New Testament translation; footnote gives ham-huār, we, Luke xv,23. Preserve this bibliographic/context claim without adding Rangri rows.
Reflexive possessive often not used, as common in Rajasthani; ordinary pronominal genitive replaces it. Preserve frequency and comparison qualification.
Source says nasals may be omitted in the third-person paradigm; current pronoun-prefix handler does not cover these section names.
Emphatic -j often added; ū̃-j wakhat explicitly illustrates it.
Both examples illustrate pleonastic k in pronominal adjectives, said to be common in Jaipuri.
Source introduces the pronominal adverb examples as pure locatives; the list continues on p57.
Continuation of source’s pure-locative pronominal adverb list.
Source qualifies lack of third-person-plural nasalization as usual in Rajasthani.
Continuation from p57: present-participle imperfect explicitly compared with Gujarati and Bundeli, unlike other Rajasthani oblique verbal-noun constructions.
Future adds gā to simple present; gā does not vary for number or gender, and follows Marwari lā. Preserve on emitted paradigms as bound-suffix audit alone does not expose it.
Source says future formations characterized by s or h do not seem to occur. Explicit Malvi variant gō compared with Bundeli varies by number/gender and remains an excluded control.
Source says causatives formed somewhat as in Marwari, often inserting ḍ after characteristic ā; Marwari inserts r. Preserve qualifications often/somewhat.

Potential passive past using ṇō is compared with Northern Gujarati; past is formally identical with infinitive. Awadhi ā-verbs compared with same past formation. Attributed analogy, not donor direction.
Intensifying j called very common and also found in Gujarati; retain claim on emitted examples.
ḍō called very common Rajasthani suffix, usually diminutive or contemptuous; lō said to have same use. Preserve class claim without asserting both meanings for each example.
